Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette: John was a 68-year-old African American widower who worked as a Policy Analyst. His life had taken an unexpected and harrowing turn when he was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness several months ago. The experience left him feeling overwhelmed and profoundly changed his daily life. The diagnosis came abruptly during one of John's routine check-ups. Initially, the symptoms seemed minor-a persistent cough, fatigue, and occasional dizziness-but they escalated quickly. He was admitted to the hospital where tests revealed a serious condition that required immediate attention. The intensity and unpredictability of the illness had left him feeling constantly tense and ready to react to any potential danger. In the months since his diagnosis, John's life had become a series of medical appointments and treatments. His body felt perpetually on high alert, as if it were still bracing for another onslaught from the disease. This constant tension made it difficult for him to concentrate at work, where he often found himself distracted by intrusive thoughts about his health. At home, John felt just as on edge. The familiarity of his surroundings no longer provided a sense of security; instead, he was acutely aware that each day could bring new challenges related to his illness. His body's reactions only heightened this feeling of vulnerability. Even when he knew he was in a safe place, the physical sensations of anxiety and tension made it hard for him to relax. John's memories of the traumatic experience were particularly distressing. Sometimes, when he tried to recall what had happened, he felt completely numb, as if the events had occurred to someone else rather than himself. Other times, the memory felt vivid and immediate, as though he was reliving the moment over again. The intensity of these recollections often overwhelmed him, forcing him to stop whatever he was doing until the wave of emotion passed. This inability to process his experiences led John to develop a series of avoidance behaviors. He avoided situations that might trigger thoughts about his illness, which included social gatherings and even familiar places associated with medical treatments. His work suffered as a result; he found himself withdrawing from team meetings and avoiding collaborations that required prolonged focus or close interaction with others. John's relationships were also strained by his symptoms. His friends and colleagues noticed the change in him but didn't fully understand what was happening. They grew concerned about his withdrawal, but John felt too overwhelmed to explain the depth of his struggles. He had come to believe that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again-a conviction that further isolated him from those around him. The realization that his body was still reacting as if it were under threat also left him feeling mistrustful and uncertain about his own physical well-being. This distrust extended beyond the illness itself; John began to question whether his body could ever be reliable, adding another layer of anxiety to his daily life. Despite these challenges, something finally pushed John to seek help. His work performance had declined significantly, and he was at risk of losing his job if things didn't improve. Additionally, he felt a growing sense of isolation that made him yearn for connection and support. He realized that he needed someone who could understand the complex emotions and physical reactions he was experiencing. In therapy, John expressed his fears about never feeling normal again and the overwhelming nature of his memories. At the same time, he hoped to regain some semblance of control over his life and find ways to manage his symptoms effectively. He looked forward to learning coping strategies that could help him navigate his daily challenges without being consumed by constant tension and fear. Through this journey, John's clinical portrait emerged as a vivid illustration of how a traumatic experience can profoundly impact one's sense of self and daily functioning. His efforts to regain control and find a way to reconnect with the world around him underscored the resilience he still possessed despite his struggles.
